title: Chapter 33 — The Specksnyder
paragraphs: Concerning the officers of the whale ship, this seems as good a place as any to describe a small domestic peculiarity on board, arising from the existence of the harpooner class of officers — a class unknown, of course, in any other service but the whale fleet.

The great importance attached to the harpooner's profession is shown by the fact that originally, in the old Dutch Fishery two centuries and more ago, command of a whale ship was not entirely in the hands of the person now called the captain. It was divided between him and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally, this word means Fat-Cutter, though in time it came to mean Chief Harpooner. In those days, the captain's authority was limited to navigation and the general management of the vessel, while over the whale-hunting department and everything related to it, the Specksnyder reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch post still exists, but with much reduced authority. At present he ranks simply as senior harpooner and is merely one of the captain's lesser subordinates. Nevertheless, since the success of a whaling voyage largely depends on the harpooners' performance, and since in the American Fishery the harpooner is not only an important officer in the boat but also, under certain circumstances like night watches on a whaling ground, has command of the ship's deck — the grand political principle of the sea demands that he should officially live apart from the common sailors and be distinguished as their professional superior, though they always regard him as their social equal.

Now, the key distinction between officer and ordinary seaman at sea is this: the officer lives aft, the seaman lives forward. Hence, on whale ships and merchant vessels alike, the mates have their quarters with the captain. And on most American whalers, the harpooners are also housed in the aft part of the ship — meaning they eat their meals in the captain's cabin and sleep in a space connected to it.

Though the long duration of a southern whaling voyage (by far the longest of all voyages ever made by man), the peculiar dangers of it, and the shared interest among a crew who all depend not on fixed wages but on common luck, vigilance, bravery, and hard work — though all these things sometimes produce a less rigid discipline than on merchant ships, and though these whalemen may in some cases live together like one big primitive family — for all that, the formal manners of the quarter-deck are seldom seriously relaxed and never entirely abandoned. Indeed, on many Nantucket ships you'll see the captain parading his quarter-deck with a lofty grandeur unmatched in any military navy — demanding nearly as much outward respect as if he wore imperial purple instead of the shabbiest pilot cloth.

And though of all captains, the moody master of the Pequod was the least given to this sort of shallow pretension — though the only obedience he ever demanded was instant and absolute — though he required no man to remove his shoes before stepping on the quarter-deck — and though there were times when, owing to special circumstances that will be described later, he spoke to his crew in unusual terms, whether condescending, threatening, or otherwise — even Captain Ahab was by no means careless about the established forms and customs of the sea.

Nor, perhaps, will it escape notice that behind those forms and customs, he sometimes masked himself, using them for other, more private purposes than they were designed for. That certain tyrannical quality in his mind, which might otherwise have stayed largely hidden, became through those forms an irresistible dictatorship made flesh. For no matter how great a man's intellectual superiority, it can never achieve practical, real-world dominance over other men without the help of some kind of external ceremony and trappings — which are always, in themselves, rather petty and base. This is what forever keeps God's true princes from the world's public stage, and awards the highest honors that this world can give to men who become famous more through their infinite inferiority to the chosen hidden few, than through any genuine superiority over the average mass. Such great power lurks in these small things, when extreme political superstition invests them, that in some royal cases they have given authority even to utter imbeciles. But when, as with Nicholas the Czar, the ringed crown of a geographic empire encircles a truly imperial brain — then the common masses cower before the tremendous power at the center. Nor will the tragic playwright who wants to depict indomitable human will in its fullest sweep ever overlook a hint so important to his art as the one I have just described.

But my Captain Ahab still stands before me in all his Nantucket grimness and roughness. And in this digression about emperors and kings, I must not forget that I am dealing only with a poor old whale hunter like him. Therefore, all outward majestic trappings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! Whatever is grand in you must be plucked from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and found in the invisible air!
